1:
The case is stated, and the manner of its statement examined first. Chrysostom contrasts this opening with the one on their divisions, where the apostle began gently: here he lays about him at once and makes the reproach as general as possible. He did not ask why such a one had committed fornication but said it is reported that there is fornication among you, so that none should take it easily as one aloof from the charge, the whole body being wounded and the Church reproached. Gill and Calvin press the publicity — Gill that the offence was in everybody’s mouth throughout Corinth and Achaia, so the church could not plead ignorance, Calvin that the adverb means no vague rumour but a matter published everywhere. Barnes and Robertson trace it to the household of Chloe.

Whether the father was living is the chapter’s first real dispute, and the witnesses take five positions. Lightfoot argues from the second epistle that he was alive: the man who did the wrong is plainly this offender, and the one who suffered it the father, of whom it would scarcely be said, if dead, that he suffered wrong. Wesley says the same. Clarke reports that most take that view on the same evidence, but decides the man had married his deceased father’s wife, a widowed stepmother. Ellicott argues from the verb, which always implies actual marriage in the New Testament, that she had been divorced from the father. Robertson denies any marriage, calling it permanent concubinage, and leaves the father dead or divorced. Henry allows either, distinguishing the cases: marrying her after the father’s death would have been incest still, though neither fornication nor adultery strictly, while taking her in his lifetime was incestuous fornication. Calvin refuses the question, since seduction and a pretended marriage are equally execrable here.

The comparison with the Gentiles is the second dispute. Chrysostom takes it strictly: the heathen not only dare no such thing but do not even give it a name. Clarke, Henry and Calvin deny it can be pressed so far, since such unions did occur: Clarke says Paul can only mean it was not accredited by them, their best writers branding it as infamous, and he and Henry both cite Cicero’s phrase for an incredible and unheard-of wickedness, while Calvin notes that tragedies were founded on such incest. Calvin also rejects the explanation that Paul named the Gentiles rather than the Jews because of Reuben, as foreign to an intention that was to heighten the aggravation. Robertson turns it on the city itself, where the very word Corinthianize meant to live in wantonness. Clarke and Ellicott add that the word rendered named is absent from almost every important manuscript.

The phrasing and the law behind it occupy three. Ellicott notes that his father’s wife is the Hebrew form for stepmother, the phraseology in which Leviticus forbids the union; Robertson records that the law prescribed stoning while the rabbis contrived a subterfuge for a proselyte, and wonders whether the Corinthians had learned that hair-splitting; Tertullian, arguing against a rival theology, concedes that by the Creator’s law the man was an offender and the apostle followed the principles of natural and public law. On their own bearing Barnes insists they were proud in spite of the scandal, not because of it, and that discipline should begin in mourning, not anger or party feeling. Ellicott would read the clause as a question and refers the pride to the earlier party rivalry; Robertson, also reading a question, is blunter: the man’s own faction justified him. Calvin gives two reasons why one man’s sin should grieve all: the communion of the members, and the stain a church contracts, as God’s anger was kindled against all Israel for Achan. Clarke and Wesley read the removal as disowning rather than execution, Clarke doubting the young church had the later forms of excommunication.
3:
Present in spirit draws three answers. Clarke suspects the gift of discerning spirits, possessed on extraordinary occasions, and Wesley a full and, it seems, miraculous view of the fact. Barnes reports that reading and declines it: the phrase does not demand a power of discerning a case at a distance, and Paul probably meant only that his mind had been given to the subject. Calvin reaches the same sense, that Paul says it lest anyone allege he judged rashly at such a distance: the duty was as plain to him as if he had seen it with his eyes. Robertson describes the construction instead: in a sentence of much difficulty the apostle seems to conceive an imaginary church court in which the offender has been tried.

Whose act the sentence is divides them sharply. Barnes takes it to prove that discipline belongs to the church itself, so deeply that even an apostle would not administer it without them, his own part being a declared opinion, not a formal sentence. Calvin presses the same into church order: Paul does not excommunicate at his own pleasure but consults the Church, so that the authority belongs to no individual; from the clause about their assembling he derives the ancient Presbytery, elders who judged first and laid the matter before the people already determined. Gill and Wesley take the opposite view — Gill that the delivering to Satan was no act of the church at all, not what they were to do or ought to do, but the apostle’s own; Wesley that the passing of this sentence was the apostle’s act and not the Corinthians’. Robertson finds the hinge in the punctuation: the clause about the Lord’s power may go with their assembling or with the infinitive to deliver, and on the first reading Paul assumes less prerogative.

Delivering to Satan is the widest dispute. Calvin reports the older reading, that the apostles could employ Satan as a scourge, so that the phrase means severe bodily punishment, as is usually said of Alexander and Hymeneus; but on comparing the second epistle he gives it up as forced, understanding the phrase simply of excommunication — for as Christ reigns within the Church, Satan reigns without, so a man cast out becomes an alien delivered to his power, a point credited to Augustine. Barnes reports that Beza and the Latin fathers made it excommunication only, Scripture recognising two kingdoms so that exclusion from one subjects a man to the other; he grants excommunication is intended, but holds the offender was thereby also exposed to bodily infliction by Satan, elsewhere the author of disease as with Job. Clarke and Gill deny that reading outright. Clarke says no evidence exists that delivering to Satan was any form of excommunication known among Jews or Christians, and that those who searched the Jewish records found nothing answering to it; it was a punishment for extraordinary cases entrusted to apostles alone, the power by which Ananias and Sapphira were struck dead, so that none remains now and pretensions to it are as wicked as vain. Gill agrees it was neither excommunication nor a form of it, that the primitive churches never so used the phrase, and that no man can do it now.

On the outcome they converge. Clarke has body and mind tortured with diseases and terrors, generally for a season though sometimes unto death, while the immortal spirit remained under divine mercy, the interference bringing the man to deep humiliation. Wesley reads the destruction as slow and gradual, preventable by speedy repentance. Robertson takes it both of physical suffering, as with Job, and of the conquest of fleshly sin, calling it remedial punishment aimed at the offender’s reformation, and denies that expulsion from a local church implies damnation. Ellicott states the aim in a line: the object was the destruction of the flesh and the man’s salvation.
6:
The proverb is applied before it is explained. Barnes says boasting is never good but especially wrong where an evil is likely to corrupt the whole church, and that men disposed to boast should ask what sin they are indulging. Calvin charges them with arrant folly in extolling themselves as though all were in a golden style while so much among them was disgraceful. Clarke and Wesley put the danger plainly — Clarke that if the leaven remains the flood-gates of impurity will open and Christianity be ruined in Corinth, Wesley that one sin or one sinner diffuses guilt through the whole congregation. Robertson notes the emphasis on the word little, and suspects some had argued that a single case did not affect the church, a specious excuse Paul answers; he compares germs of disease spreading through a body.

What is to be purged is disputed. Clarke reads the command straight at the man: as the Jews search their houses before the passover, so act with this person. Ellicott denies it outright: not the offending man is spoken of but the spirit in the Church which tolerated the evil, purged out that they may become what by profession they are. Barnes takes both, meaning by the old leaven vice and sin and also the man who committed it. Gill offers both without choosing: either the incestuous person, whose removal is properly the church’s act of excommunication and quite distinct from what the apostle would do himself, or the church’s own old course of sinning. Henry divides it the same way, between the body expelling a scandalous member and each member purging his own heart. Calvin observes that Paul has left the case of incest for a general exhortation. Robertson notes the aorist’s urgency: do it now, before the whole church is contaminated.

The passover imagery is filled out and its occasion debated. Gill describes the search the Jews made by lamplight on the night of the fourteenth of Nisan, in every secret place and corner, as Barnes does with candles; Ellicott says that as the Jew removed every atom when the paschal lamb was eaten, so no moral leaven may remain now that our Paschal Lamb is slain. Whether Paul wrote at that season is another question. Clarke thinks the passover was approaching and that the apostle takes advantage of it; Ellicott, reasoning from the letter’s date shortly before Pentecost, thinks it was about or soon after Easter, which is why the figures suggested themselves. Robertson grants the possibility and then guards it: if so it is merely incidental, and the language here is not a plea for the observance of Easter by Christians. Ellicott adds that the words rendered for us are absent from the best manuscripts, the verb meaning simply to slay.

What the feast now is divides them again. Gill denies it is the passover, now ceased, though the language alludes to it. Barnes agrees it is neither the paschal supper nor the Lord’s Supper, but the putting away of all evil from hearts and churches. Wesley finds the sacrament plainly here, taking the feast as feeding on Christ by faith and the Supper as instituted in the room of the passover. Robertson reads the tense as continuous, a perpetual feast with the leaven kept out, and Ellicott likewise makes the whole of time a festival to Christians. Calvin turns the verse against the mass, since Paul does not teach that Christ is offered daily, and insists the ancient passover was not merely a memorial of a past benefit but a sacrament representing the Christ who was to come. Clarke reads the unleavened bread of the clause as upright and godly men. Calvin and Wesley pause over the transition, admiring as exquisite skill the way the apostle slides from the incestuous man to a crucified Saviour, and both reach for the bold yet natural transitions of Pindar.
9:
Which letter Paul means is the standing question, and Clarke stands almost alone. Calvin says the epistle is not extant and that many others are lost, those preserved being what the Lord foresaw would suffice; Robertson agrees, and wishes a bundle of papyri in Egypt might give it back. Gill adds that the loss detracts nothing from the perfection of Scripture, since not all the apostle wrote was by divine inspiration, and that the letter was lost or neglected, so the reminder is a reproof. Clarke denies the whole account: those best skilled in criticism agree no other epistle is meant, the aorist standing for a pluperfect, so the sense is I had written to you in this epistle; the inference of a lost letter is not legitimately drawn from the text or from antiquity, though he grants the second epistle tells against him and allows that Paul may refer to a letter written but suppressed on fresh news. Barnes sets out the division by name and decides for the lost one; Henry reports both and refuses to regret the loss, the revelation being entire in the books that have come down to us.

Why the qualification was needed is explained before it is examined. Chrysostom reconstructs the danger: told to mourn and purge out the leaven, they would suppose they must avoid every fornicator, reasoning that if a sinning friend is not spared much less an outsider — whereupon they would have separated from the Greeks too, found it impossible, and taken it the harder. So Paul concedes the point as though acknowledged, showing the course impossible however much they wished.

What the concession means divided the interpreters, and Calvin lists them. Some read it as saying they must sooner quit Greece; Ambrose, that they must rather die; Erasmus turns it into a wish that they might leave the world altogether but, being unable, must quit the society of those who falsely take the name of Christian. Calvin prefers Chrysostom’s exposition, that Paul forbids company only with fornicators who wish to be regarded as brethren, lest sufferance seem approval, and takes the world here of the present life. The others reach the same place by shorter roads. Barnes says the prohibition never meant refusing civility or the ordinary transactions of life, but refusing to make such men companions and friends. Ellicott says literal obedience would have required withdrawing from business, and that Paul guards the fair fame of the Church, which is to be the light of the world and not the recipient of its darkness. Robertson puts it as jurisdiction: the rule is confined to members, since Paul has none over outsiders. Wesley is blunt: going out of the world, which some account a perfection, Paul accounts an utter absurdity. Clarke draws the darker inference, that the Corinthians could not transact ordinary business with any others, there being none others in that city.

The list itself draws comment. Ellicott finds idolater strange here, since a brother could hardly worship images, and supposes it carries the sensuality attending heathen worship; Barnes takes it of professors who still attended the idol feasts. Robertson glosses the covetous as over-reachers who always come in bad company, and the extortioners as grafters; he notes that the aorist here is epistolary, unlike the one two verses earlier, and reports that Chrysostom knew people who objected to revilers and drunkards in such company, theirs being the more respectable vices. Calvin rejects as forced the construction referring the clause to what follows, while granting the sentiment drawn from it is just, that none can be punished by the Church but one whose sin is notorious. Clarke and Wesley end on the practical rule: worldly concerns may be transacted with a man who makes no profession, whatever his character, but not with a scandalous professor; and refusing even to eat withholds the lowest degree of familiarity.
12:
The limitation is stated plainly by most, questioned by one. Barnes says Paul has no jurisdiction over those outside, so that all his rules must refer only to those within; Robertson puts it in a line, that they are outside the church and God judges them; Wesley reduces it to a sentence, that he speaks of Christians only. Ellicott adds that the verse explains the grounds of the limitation and hints that the Corinthians ought to have seen it applied only to their own body. Calvin qualifies rather than repeats: nothing hinders us from judging outsiders too, since not even devils are exempt from the judgment of the word committed to us, but Paul speaks of the jurisdiction peculiar to the Church, chastisement being a discipline confined to the household and not extending to strangers, so that we must leave them to the judgment of God.

Lightfoot will not have the received sense. He notes that the versions agree in making it a disclaimer — what does it concern me, what have I to do — and grants that the Greek phrase very often carries that force; but he presses an objection from the apostle’s own practice. If it did not concern him to judge those without, why did he judge Elymas with blindness, and why Hymeneus and Alexander by delivering them to Satan, when they were now apostates and no other than such as were without? He therefore proposes another rendering: why is power granted me to judge them also that are without, that is, to strike even a heathen with some divine plague if he be incorrigible. Clarke, without addressing Lightfoot, removes the very word on which the difficulty turns, reporting that also is wanting in many manuscripts and in the Syriac, Coptic, Slavonic, Vulgate and Itala as well as several fathers, and saying it greatly disturbs the sense; with it gone he reads a plain question and denial, followed by the charge to judge those within. Clarke and Ellicott agree that those without was a common Jewish name for the Gentile world.

What becomes of the outsiders is answered alike, coloured differently. Gill says God will judge them in the great day, so that though they fall under neither the apostle’s censure nor a church’s they will not go unpunished, the saints meanwhile having only to watch over one another and reprove as cases require. Barnes says they are under the direct and peculiar government of God, ours being the church alone. Wesley says the sentence on these God has reserved to himself. Ellicott notes that the best manuscripts put the verb in the future, God will judge, and leaves the heathen world in the hands of the judge of the whole earth. Calvin’s version is harsher: God allows them to wander unbridled like wild beasts, there being none to restrain their wantonness.

The closing sentence raises one more disagreement. Robertson says the quotation from Deuteronomy clinches the case for expulsion, and Clarke traces the same words to the direction given to Israel about idolatry; Ellicott observes that the apostle adopts the form in which sentence was pronounced on great criminals, familiar to the Jewish converts, and would omit the opening word therefore. Barnes takes excommunication to be the utmost power the church has and one it is bound to exercise; Wesley says simply that this properly belongs to them. Calvin reports the common explanation, that the wicked person is the man guilty of the illicit connection, and disposes of a rival reading making it the wicked thing, since the Greek article is masculine. Then his own suggestion: what if the phrase refers to the devil, who in the person of an unprincipled man is encouraged to set up his throne among us, since the wicked one taken without addition denotes the prince of all crimes rather than some wicked man?
